title: Celandine and the Sad Dragon
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks had a worry with height. Summits scraped cloud. The Sunstone, which kept their glow, had gone. Elder Maeve’s face, a map of mountain winters, creased.

“The Sunstone Ceremony is almost here,” she said, voice like rustling leaves. “Who will brave the Sky-Rope Bridges for Ignis, the Dragon of Crimson Peak?”

Celandine stepped forward, moss-green cloak dusted with herbs. Whisk, a sleek stoat, thumped his tail. She held a small carved wooden bird, wings ready. “I have a plan.”

A swirl of glitter and a wind that smelled of sugared violets announced Iseult Buttercup, a witch whose spells looked grander than they felt. Her robes shimmered as if they had opinions.

“Magic is the answer!” Iseult boomed. She conjured a flock of dazzling sky-sheep, bleating like tinkling bells. “They’ll distract Ignis while I snatch the stone!”

The sky-sheep only annoyed Ignis. The dragon, scales like embers, rumbled a sigh that shook the peak. Sheep scattered like dandelion fluff. Iseult’s rainbow bridge sputtered out and left her sputtering too, face puce. Maeve sighed, a pine-wind sound, and turned to Celandine.

“Your turn.”

“Patience now,” Celandine told Whisk. The Sky-Rope Bridges swayed like spiderwebs over chasms that ate sky. Whisk darted ahead, testing planks. Celandine followed. Quiet work. Her sort.

A gust sharp as a giant’s sneeze tore the pass. A vital rope snapped—thunder and twigs. The bridge sagged, a broken tooth, and stranded them. Crimson Peak looked farther than geography allowed.

Celandine found a hidden goat trail, a shy serpent up the mountainside. “This way.” Thorns snagged cloaks like tiny fingers. They came out on a ledge before a cave mouth glowing warm as cooling embers.

Inside, Ignis lay curled over sparkling rock. The Sunstone sat on a high ledge, light dimmed. He was not roaring. He was sniffling. Less monster than sad puppy in armour.

“She called my scales dull,” Ignis mumbled, a rumble of hurt. A tear, hot as a coal, ran down. “And my roar sounded like indigestion. I have delicate feelings.”

Celandine’s acorn-brown eyes widened. Iseult’s magic had not outsmarted him. It had bruised him. The broken rope was what rushing bought. She knelt slowly.

“Your scales shine like a thousand sunsets,” she said. “Your roar is the mountain singing. But you seem very sad.”

Ignis looked up, golden eyes full. “No one asks if I’m sad. They just want the stone. They see me and think monster.” He nudged the Sunstone. “It’s heavy. And lonely. I just want a friend.”

Celandine stroked the velvety nose. Whisk hopped onto a paw and sniffed scales with a soft squeak.

“We haven’t had tea,” Celandine said, “and tea solves many things.” She produced a tin of dried cloudberries, plump and sweet. Ignis nibbled, snout twitching. “The Sunstone belongs where it can brighten the Peaks. You deserve kindness. We can bring stories. And more cloudberries, if you like.”

Ignis blinked, slow as a sunset. He looked at the stone, then at the witch and the stoat now curled on his flank. A gentle rumble. With infinite care he nudged the Sunstone into Celandine’s hands.

The way back was easier. Ignis promised to watch the bridges. Celandine presented the stone to Maeve; a faint warm pulse lived in her pouch. Whisk had kept a small pebble warmed by dragon-breath, a token with no speech attached. Iseult, somewhere below, was still explaining sky-sheep to anyone who would not listen.

The Peaks took their glow back. Celandine put the carved bird on a shelf and left the window open, in case a friend with ember scales wanted cloudberries again.
characters: Celandine (witch of the Whispering Peaks), Whisk (stoat companion), Ignis (a mountain dragon with surprisingly delicate feelings)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
author: StoryGen Community
